The countdown and weekly info need the first day of your last period to estimate a due date — more accurate than entering a due date directly.

string-array.name: home_daily_messages
string-array.item: A little longer, and you\'ll be three.
Every day that passes is a day closer to her.
Take a deep breath. You\'re more ready than you think.
She\'s already waiting to meet you.
The house is almost ready. Your hearts already were.
One more moon, and your biggest adventure begins.

string-array.name: home_weekly_info
string-array.item: Pregnancy is counted from week 1 starting on the first day of the last period, before ovulation and fertilization actually happen. Still too early for symptoms — mostly a time to start tracking.
Ovulation happens around this week, and if fertilization occurs, it\'s happening right now, usually in the fallopian tube.
The fertilized egg divides repeatedly on its way to the uterus, and within a few days will implant in the uterine lining. This is still very much the beginning.
Implantation in the uterine lining is complete, and the body starts releasing the hCG hormone that home pregnancy tests detect.
The neural tube, which will become the brain and spinal cord, begins forming. The embryonic heart starts beating irregularly.
The heart beats more regularly and can sometimes be seen on ultrasound. The beginnings of arm and leg joints start to appear.
The brain develops rapidly, and early facial features begin forming — including spots that will become the eyes and nostrils.
All the vital internal organs already exist in basic form and keep developing. The fingers begin separating from each other.
The embryo starts moving, even if not yet felt. Muscles begin developing and the body gradually straightens from its curled position.
The fetal period officially begins this week — the basic organs exist and continue growing and maturing. Fingernails begin forming.
The body grows faster than the head, which until now was relatively large. Fingers and toes are no longer webbed together.
First reflexes develop — the fingers can curl. The kidneys begin producing urine that mixes into the amniotic fluid.
End of the first trimester. The whoosh of the fetal heartbeat becomes clearer on checkups. Fingerprints are starting to form.
Facial features sharpen, and the fetus starts making facial movements like frowning. The baby\'s sex can sometimes be identified.
Bones keep hardening, and the fetus starts sensing light through still-closed eyelids. The sense of hearing begins developing.
You may start feeling first fetal movements ("kicks") — still gentle and flutter-like. The skeleton keeps hardening.
The first fat tissue starts accumulating under the skin. The placenta keeps growing and strengthening to support development.
The ears are in their final position and start hearing sounds from outside — including your voice. You may feel movements more clearly.
A waxy protective coating (vernix) starts covering the skin. The senses of taste, smell, hearing, sight and touch begin differentiating in brain regions.
Halfway there! You may have a detailed anatomy scan around this week, and the baby\'s sex can often be identified clearly.
Movements become stronger and more noticeable. The digestive system starts functioning in a basic way, and eyelashes and eyelids are developed.
The fetus starts developing a sense of touch — touching its face and the umbilical cord. The skin is still thin and wrinkled, before fat forms underneath.
The lungs develop branching airways, in preparation for future breathing. Changes in air pressure or loud noise may trigger a fetal reaction.
Sometimes considered a medical "viability threshold," though continued pregnancy remains critical for lung and brain development. The sense of balance begins developing.
Fine hair (lanugo) covers parts of the body and helps regulate temperature. The placenta keeps supplying nutrition and oxygen at a growing rate.
The eyes start opening for the first time. The lungs keep producing surfactant — a substance that will later enable independent breathing.
End of the second trimester. The brain is very active and produces brain-wave patterns, and sleep-wake cycles start forming.
Eyelashes are full and eyelids can open and close. The fetus responds to light, sound and tastes in the amniotic fluid.
The brain and skeleton keep developing rapidly, so the need for calcium, protein and iron in the diet increases during this period.
The eyes can now track light. Bone marrow has fully taken over red blood cell production from the liver and spleen.
Movements may feel strong but less spacious — simply because things are getting more crowded in there. The lungs and brain keep maturing rapidly.
Fingernails already reach the fingertips. The baby\'s weight rises quickly as fat tissue accumulates under the skin.
The baby starts practicing breathing. A good time to start packing the hospital bag.
The lungs keep developing and the baby is likely already head-down. Worth making sure the car seat is installed.
Birth weight is nearly set from now on. A good time to finish the urgent items on the shopping list.
Considered almost "full term." Worth finalizing the route to the hospital and making sure important documents are ready and accessible.
The baby is officially considered "full term"! She could arrive any moment — the hospital bag should be by the door.
Most organs are fully mature. A good time to finish last errands at home and rest as much as possible.
The baby keeps gaining weight and is ready to arrive any day. Worth making sure important phone numbers are accessible to both of you.
The estimated due date has arrived. Remember: most babies aren\'t born exactly on their due date, and that\'s completely normal.
